problem: The lead says the spreading of the force creates both bursting and spalling ("This spreading creates transverse tension ... called bursting, and small surface tension, called spalling"). Spalling is not caused by the spreading of the force. It is a local effect at the loaded face, where the stiff bearing plate restrains the lateral expansion of the concrete around it, so tension appears on planes parallel to the loaded face just outside the plate. The chapter's own Q4 answer contradicts the lead: it says a larger plate (which reduces spreading) still leaves spalling to be dealt with.
fix: Spreading of the force produces bursting tension behind the plate. A separate local effect, spalling tension, appears in the concrete around the plate at the loaded face, because the plate restrains the lateral expansion of the concrete beneath it. Both must be dealt with, but they have different causes.

problem: Ast ≈ Fbst / (0.87 fy) does not state the units to be used. With fy in N/mm², Fbst must be in N. A student who puts Fbst in kN (as the worked example and Q3 report it) gets an Ast that is 1000 times too small.
fix: Write: Ast ≈ Fbst / (0.87 fy), with Fbst in N, fy in N/mm² and Ast in mm². Convert Fbst from kN to N before using the formula, e.g. 166.7 kN = 166,700 N.

problem: Section 2 defines P as the anchorage force after losses, but Section 3 and the worked example use P without saying what it is (jack force or force after losses). The bursting force and bearing stress both change with the force chosen.
fix: State in Section 3 and in the example that P is the anchorage force after losses (the jack force reduced by losses), and that the same value is used for the bearing and bursting checks.

problem: For a rectangular plate the formula uses a and b in one direction only. The chapter never says that bursting must be checked separately in each direction, with a and b taken as the plate and end-block dimensions in that direction.
fix: Add: for a rectangular plate, repeat the bursting check in both directions, taking a and b in the same direction each time, and provide stirrups for the larger of the two bursting forces in each direction.
